extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, inventors, small businesses, policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria on patent-system policy and best practices for filing and prosecuting patent applications (grace periods, provisional filings, PTO funding, examination priorities, and litigation-related provisions). Useful to practitioners advising inventors and policymakers drafting legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of first-inventor-to-file system
rubrics_metrics.description: Move from first-to-invent to first-inventor-to-file is acceptable if paired with safeguards (a real and substantial grace period and retained rights to swear behind references for certain prior art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data (e.g., only 7 cases favoring individuals in 2007) suggests a de facto first-to-file regime already exists; switching reduces interference proceedings and simplifies the system for independent inventors. Encourage filing earlier; argue that simplicity benefits inventors who otherwise misunderstand first-to-invent rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve a 12-month grace period
rubrics_metrics.description: Retain a real and substantial 12-month grace period so inventors and start-ups can disclose and still obtain patents if they file within 12 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed S.23 102(b) contains a narrower grace period than current law; critics claiming 'no grace period' are mistaken. Concern that proposed language limits protection (does not extend to all third-party activities). Law should preserve broad, predictable protection currently enjoyed under 102(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear statutory definition of 'disclosure'
rubrics_metrics.description: Statute must define 'disclosure' explicitly because proposed 102(b) lacks a definition, leaving uncertainty about what activities (public use, sale, publication) count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventors and start-ups worry whether their own public use or sale activities fall within the exception; lack of definition creates uncertainty and could erode the grace period's practical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain ability to swear behind references
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserve applicants' right to 'swear behind' references to demonstrate earlier date of invention, at least for prior art not arising from earlier-filed patent applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping this right helps inventors who disclosed or otherwise have evidence of earlier invention date; incorporated as a safeguard when moving to first-inventor-to-file.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional application sufficiency — substance over form
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional patent application must be complete as to disclosure (enablement/written description) but need not meet nonprovisional formalities; substance matters more than formal structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional filings need enough disclosure that someone skilled in the art understands the invention. They do not need to be identical to nonprovisionals. Avoid 'crappy' provisionals, but a well-crafted provisional (often drafted by an attorney) is a valid and cost-effective way to secure a filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention notebook standards — provable conception and diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Invention notebooks or records should identify conception and dates with sufficient detail that others skilled in the art understand what was invented and when, enabling proof of conception and diligence if needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many inventor-supplied disclosures are inadequate (often one-paragraph). Reliable notebooks must be detailed enough to support a claim of conception; however, attorney-drafted provisionals are typically superior to cryptic notes. If relying on first-to-invent, maintain rigorous records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage early filing as strategic best practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventors (especially independents and start-ups) should file patent applications earlier in the development process to avoid losing rights under a first-inventor-to-file regime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-to-file systems incentivize earlier filing; provisional applications are positioned as a low-cost, fast tool to stake an early claim. The argument that provisional filing is too costly is countered by advocating streamlined provisional strategies and attorney assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional drafting and prosecution workflow
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred drafting workflow: prepare thorough specification/description first (text), then translate into claim language; perform prior art search, patentability assessment, mapping, and identify base target and alternative embodiments to support multiple claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach (spec first, then claims) aids in creating a detailed specification supporting numerous claim sets. The 80-20 rule analogy: initial broad descriptive work takes less time, while final claim drafting and detailed linking consumes more time; use this to plan efficient provisional/nonprovisional preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: End fee diversion — ensure PTO retains user fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Stop diverting patent and trademark user fees from the PTO to the Treasury/other purposes; allow the PTO to retain and use fees to address backlog and improve operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fee diversion (hundreds of millions diverted historically) starves the PTO of resources. Ending diversion (e.g., via a revolving fund) would let the PTO allocate funds to reduce pendency, hire examiners, and improve service to inventors and businesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable PTO funding model and potential fee-setting authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a stable and sustainable funding model for the PTO, potentially allowing the Office to structure or set fees while retaining Congressional oversight and accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Director testimony noted need for predictable funding. Allowing PTO to set fees could improve efficiency but must be balanced with oversight to prevent inefficiency or overcharging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce backlog and shorten pendency
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative and funding measures should aim to substantially reduce the patent application backlog and shorten pendency (time to first action and final disposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High backlog numbers (e.g., 718,000 waiting for first action; average pendency ~36 months) harm inventors and innovation. Directing retained fees to hiring examiners and process improvements is recommended to achieve timely examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary PTO proceeding for business-method patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Institute a temporary administrative proceeding at the PTO to reexamine certain business-method patents as a middle-ground reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach can balance concerns of the financial and tech communities and provide an expedited mechanism to address problematic business-method claims without full-scale litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid congressional changes to damages and venue (promote certainty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from enacting statutory changes to damages and venue that could introduce more uncertainty; allow court development (e.g., Federal Circuit) to continue maturing these doctrines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some Senators advocated striking damages and venue provisions from the bill to preserve certainty; courts have been moving in a direction that may render legislative intervention unnecessary or disruptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small-entity fee relief for accelerated examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide fee reductions (e.g., 50% reduction) for small businesses seeking accelerated patent examination to improve access for resource-constrained innovators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including a reduced fee for accelerated applications supports small business competitiveness and helps them engage with faster prosecution without prohibitive costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritized examination for technologies important to competitiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer prioritized/expedited examination for technologies deemed important to American competitiveness (e.g., via statutory provision Sec.18).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritized examination can accelerate protection for critical technologies and strengthen national innovation and economic goals; statutory mechanisms can designate which technologies qualify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonize only where it improves the system
rubrics_metrics.description: Harmonization with international patent practices is acceptable, but only adopt changes that demonstrably improve the U.S. system rather than harmonizing for its own sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goal should be to harmonize what the world does better and lobby others to adopt U.S. strengths, rather than wholesale adoption of foreign rules that may weaken domestic policies (e.g., grace period protections).
